wger:1476.name: Butterfly Sit Up
wger:1476.description: In this midrange exercise your arm muscles provide you with a little bit of momentum to help to get you off the ground. You also open them up in overhead position which engages the upper back. Start lying with feet flat on the ground, knees at an angle, arms crossed in towards your chest. Using your ab muscles, bring your upper body off the ground as you open your arms into goal post position, then slowly lower yourself back down to return to starting position.

wger:1477.name: Seated Corkscrew
wger:1477.description: To do this abs and obliques exercise, start with your hands back behind your body and bring your knees in and across, really trying to contract the obliques. Then extend your legs back out to starting position and repeat toward the opposite side of the abs. Beginners might find that they can’t even get through the first 45 seconds of this challenging reverse crunches variation.  That’s ok because it gives you a place to start and something to improve upon.

wger:1478.name: Levitation Crunch
wger:1478.description: For this top down movement, we’re trying to move the upper torso without moving the lower torso. Start lying on the ground with feet flat on the floor and crossed arms above your head with hands behind head. Lift upper body up and clear your shoulder blades off the ground and then hold and pause at the top for a one or two count. Try to make the upper abs work and hold that contraction for 10 good quality reps.

wger:1479.name: Sit Up Elbow Thrust
wger:1479.description: This is a top down rotation movement, and it’s a bit more explosive, too. Lying with knees bent and feet on the floor, sit up and then drive your left elbow across your entire body toward the right, then come back to center and then finally lower yourself down. Then hit the other side.

wger:1480.name: Lying Triceps Extensions
wger:1480.description:
1. Starting position for this practical triceps exercise is lying on a standard bench holding a barbell or two dumbbells in both hands with an overhand grip, hands at shoulder width apart.
  2. Begin with arms over your upper chest and elbows bent back at about a 45-degree angle.
  3. First bend at the elbows and then allow the upper arm to drop back, bringing the barbell/dumbbells behind your head and down toward the floor. In terms of upper arm position, the barbell/dumbbells should never be fully above your head, but instead behind it, to ensure that you’re targeting the triceps.
  4. Keep the shoulder blades tucked under, the elbows tight in toward your head and your core active during this entire movement.

wger:1481.name: Drag Pushdown
wger:1481.description:
1. Starting position for this rope pushdown is standing facing a cable machine with the handles of a rope attachment in both hands and feet shoulder width apart.
  2. Hinge forward slightly at the hips maintaining an upright chest and bring the shoulders and elbows behind the body so that when you push down on the cable attachments, you can get a fully contracted triceps long head.
  3. Drag the cable machine rope attachment as close to the body as possible and straighten your elbows until lockout.

wger:1482.name: Dumbbell Cheat Curl
wger:1482.description:
1. Starting position is standing with feet shoulder width apart.
  2. Hands should take an underhand or supinated grip on the dumbbells holding them with hands shoulder width apart.
  3. Keeping elbows tucked into your sides throughout the entire movement, use momentum to curl the dumbbells, squeezing your biceps at the top of the movement.
  4. Slowly lower to return to the starting position. Keep the core tight throughout the exercise.

Cheating through the concentric curling portion of this challenging exercise gives us a great opportunity to increase time under tension and create eccentric overload with heavier weight when we lower.

wger:1483.name: Bizeps Curls Trifecta
wger:1483.description:
This exercise is a mixture of three different curls: the Supinated Cross Body Curl, the Pronated Cross Body Curl and the No Money Curl. You alternate between three curl variations that each accomplish different goals, and you’ll keep the set going beyond the usual 8-12 rep range which gives us that intensity.

  1. For the Supinated Cross Body Curl, supinate the forearm with palms facing toward the ceiling and forearms coming across the body. Lift the inner-facing weight of the dumbbell towards your shoulder.
  2. For the Pronated Cross Body Curl, pronate the forearm with palms facing toward the floor (pronated grip or overhand grip) and forearms coming across the body. Lift the inner-facing weight of the dumbbell towards your shoulder.
  3. For the No Money Curl, you’ll curl the dumbbell as you outwardly rotate the shoulder. Lift the inner-facing weight of the dumbbell towards your outer side of the shoulder.

wger:1484.name: Omni Cable Cross-over
wger:1484.description:
Adjust the weights based on the motion. When pulling from top to bottom, increase the weight by 20% to 40% more than the bottom-to-top motion. This accounts for the fact that when operating from top down, the upper chest muscles are naturally weaker than the lower chest muscles. So, adjust your weight stack to compensate.

  1. Position one cable at a high setting and the other at the lowest level setting. Get into a staggered stance in between the cable towers.
  2. For the cable set low, pull it upward and across your body. This effectively targets the upper chest.
  3. For the cable set high, draw it downward and across your body. This will primarily engage the lower chest.

Once you’re done, swap the positions of the cables. Change the previously high cable to the lowest position and vice versa. Repeat the exercise sequence, ensuring you’re targeting both chest regions effectively.

wger:1485.name: Rocking Triceps Pushdown
wger:1485.description: Set your feet below the rope and lean your upper body towards the rope. Set one foot back. Push down the rope and lean your entire body back onto the rear foot as you push down to get your hands behind your body. Don't forget to bring your chest to the front during the pushdown. As you release the rope slowly, lean your body back onto the front foot.

wger:1486.name: Alternating High Cable Row
wger:1486.description:
1. Start by putting the attachment in a high position on the cable station and step back about 1m from the attachment. Grab the cable pulley handle in your left hand at about head height with your elbow slightly bent. Step back with your left foot.
  2. Pull your elbow joint in toward the torso twisting slightly and perform a single-arm row. Engage the lats as you twist.
  3. Return to the starting position with cable pulley and left foot and grab the cable pulley handle in the right hand. Repeat this motion on the opposite side with your right foot stepped back.

  3. Then raise up again with arms in a Y position to activate the lower traps.

Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the initial position. Initial position corresponds to an rectangular position of upper and lower arms.

wger:1512.name: Drop Curl
wger:1512.description: Drop curls in a modified position at a slow pace effectively engage the brachialis for arm width. Starting position is with both arms in a slight angle towards each other at chest height with a dumbbell in each hand. Lower one dumbbell close to full extended arm position slowly and in a controlled manner during the first half of the curl, then curl it back up to starting position, while the other dumbbell stays at its starting position. Now lower the other dumbbell down. This keeps tension on the brachialis. As we pass the 90deg mark on our way down, the biceps will take over the work.

wger:1519.name: Overhead Triceps Extension
wger:1519.description:
Overhead Triceps Extension with EZ Bar – Quick Guide

The overhead position emphasizes the long head of the triceps (because it's stretched under load), the exercise does engage all three triceps heads (long, lateral, and medial) to some degree during extension.

  1. Setup: Sit on a bench (or stand) and hold an EZ bar with a narrow, overhand grip. Lift the bar overhead, arms fully extended. Keep your core tight and elbows close to your head.
  2. Execution: Slowly lower the bar behind your head by bending your elbows until they reach ~90°. Keep elbows pointed forward (not flaring out).
  3. Finish: Extend your arms back up to the starting position, squeezing your triceps at the top.

Tips:

  • Control the movement to avoid straining your shoulders.
  • Use a moderate weight for full range of motion.
  • Keep your back straight and avoid arching.

wger:1525.name: Ball Slams
wger:1525.description:
1. Stand with your feet about shoulder-width apart, your knees and hips slightly bent, holding the ball in both hands at chest height. Engage your core, and keep a good posture.
  2. Extend your knees and drive your hips forward while simultaneously lifting the ball. Aim for being as tall as possible, the ball overhead, arms up, hips slightly forward, and on your toes from the force of your drive.
  3. Use your core and arms to slam the medicine ball straight down between your feet with as much force as possible. Press your hips back and bend your knees to further power the slam. Exhale as you slam the ball down.
  4. Squat down to pick up the ball from the floor, then immediately move into the next slam by repeating the movement. Repeat for reps or time.

wger:1545.name: Archer Pull Up
wger:1545.description:
An archer pull-up is an advanced bodyweight exercise that strengthens your back and biceps, serving as a progression towards a one-arm pull-up. It gets its name from the "bow-drawing" position your body takes at the top.Here's how to do it:

  1. Grip: Grasp a pull-up bar with a wider-than-shoulder-width overhand grip.
  2. Starting Position: Hang with arms fully extended, engaging your core and keeping your shoulder blades pulled down.
  3. The Pull: Pull your body up towards one hand, similar to a regular pull-up. At the same time, extend the other arm out to the side, keeping it as straight as possible. Your chin should come towards the hand that is pulling.
  4. Hold & Lower: Briefly hold the top position where one arm is bent and pulling, and the other is extended. Slowly lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
  5. Alternate: Repeat the movement, pulling up towards the opposite hand.The key to this exercise is to keep the assisting arm as straight as possible to maximise the load on the working arm. This makes it a challenging but effective exercise for unilateral pulling strength.

wger:1551.name: Push-Up
wger:1551.description:
The push-up is a fundamental bodyweight exercise that targets the chest, arms, and shoulders while engaging the core for stability. It requires no equipment and is excellent for building upper body strength.

Instructions:

  1. Start in a plank position with hands placed slightly wider than shoulder-width, feet together, and body in a straight line from head to heels.
  2. Engage your core and lower your body by bending your elbows, keeping them close to your body or flared slightly outward.
  3. Lower until your chest nearly touches the ground while maintaining a neutral spine.
  4. Push through your palms to return to the starting position, fully extending your arms.

wger:1554.name: Clap Push-UP
wger:1554.description:
The clap push-up is an explosive upper body movement that builds power and fast-twitch muscle strength. It adds a plyometric challenge to the traditional push-up by requiring the hands to leave the ground mid-rep.

  1. Start in a strong push-up position with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width and core engaged
  2. Lower your body explosively and push off the ground with enough force to lift your hands.
  3. Quickly clap your hands together at chest level before returning them to the floor.
  4. Land with soft elbows to absorb the impact and immediately move into the next rep

wger:1556.name: Devil’s Press
wger:1556.description:
The Devil’s Press is a hybrid movement combining a dumbbell burpee and a double dumbbell snatch. It’s a full-body, high-intensity exercise that develops strength, power, and metabolic conditioning.

  1. Start with a dumbbell in each hand and perform a burpee, letting your chest touch the ground while holding the dumbbells.
  2. Explosively jump your feet forward and swing the dumbbells between your legs.
  3. Drive the dumbbells overhead in one continuous motion, locking out your arms.
  4. Lower the dumbbells with control to return to the starting position and repeat

wger:1572.name: Bird Dog
wger:1572.description:
The Bird Dog is a core stability exercise that enhances balance, coordination, and spinal alignment. It’s a low-impact movement ideal for strengthening the posterior chain and improving overall functional control.

  1. Begin on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips, keeping your spine neutral.
  2. Extend your right arm forward and left leg backward simultaneously, keeping hips square.
  3. Pause briefly at full extension while engaging your core and glutes.
  4. Return to the starting position and repeat on the opposite side

wger:1576.name: Snap Down
wger:1576.description: Begin in a standing position with your arms up over your head and your toes pushing into the ground raising your heels up becoming as tall as you can. From this position, perform a small hop with both feet slightly coming off of the ground. As you land, bend your knees and begin to hinge forward at your hips absorbing the landing. Return to the starting position and repeat.  You should feel the muscles in your lower body working.  Start with your arms and knees fully straightened out. Keep a stable balance as you land and briefly hold that end position, don’t go too fast and become off balanced. Keep your chest up.  For a detailed video on landing mechanics, click here: https://youtu.be/RThUCYRDyZw

wger:1577.name: Bretzel stretch
wger:1577.description: How to Perform the Bretzel Stretch    Starting Position:        Lie on your back on a flat surface, such as a mat.        Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the ground.    Leg Positioning:        Lift your right leg and cross it over your left leg, placing your right foot on the outside of your left knee.        Your left leg should remain flat on the ground.    Arm Positioning:        Extend your left arm out to the side at shoulder height, keeping it straight.        Use your right hand to gently pull your right knee towards the floor on the left side of your body.    Stretching:        As you pull your knee down, try to keep your left shoulder flat on the ground.        You should feel a stretch in your hip, lower back, and possibly your chest.    Hold the Position:        Maintain this position for 20-30 seconds, breathing deeply and relaxing into the stretch.        Switch sides and repeat the process.

wger:1578.name: Hip hinge
wger:1578.description: Hip Hinge Exercise DescriptionThe hip hinge is a fundamental movement pattern that involves bending at the hips while keeping the spine neutral. It is commonly used in exercises like deadlifts, kettlebell swings, and good mornings. To perform a hip hinge:    Starting Position: Stand with your feet hip-width apart and a slight bend in your knees.    Hinge at the Hips: Push your hips back while maintaining a straight back. Your torso should lean forward, and your chest should stay up.    Lowering Phase: Continue to hinge until your torso is nearly parallel to the ground, or until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.    Return to Standing: Drive through your heels and thrust your hips forward to return to the starting position.

wger:1604.name: Sliding Lateral Lunge
wger:1604.description: Stand upright with your feet hip-width apart, holding a kettlebell close to your chest in goblet position. Place one foot on a slider, gliding disc, or towel. Keep your chest tall and core engaged. Slowly slide the foot outward to the side while bending the opposite knee, lowering your hips into a lateral lunge. Keep the working leg’s knee aligned with the toes and avoid letting it collapse inward. The non-working leg remains straight and slides smoothly along the floor. Push through the heel of the bent leg to return to the starting position while maintaining control of the kettlebell.

wger:1605.name: Copenhagen Adduction Exercise
wger:1605.description: Lie on your side with the elbow placed directly under the shoulder, similar to a side plank position. Place the upper leg on a bench with the inside of the foot or ankle resting on it. Lift your hips and hold your body in a straight line while keeping the lower leg off the floor. The exercise strongly activates the adductors of the upper leg while also challenging the core and hip stabilizers.

wger:1606.name: Arm Raises (T/Y/I)
wger:1606.description:
Stand upright with feet hip-width apart, core engaged, and arms relaxed at your sides. From this position, perform three different arm raises to target the shoulders and upper back:

  • T Raise: Lift your arms straight out to the sides until they are parallel to the floor, forming a “T” shape.
  • Y Raise: Lift your arms upward at about a 45° angle from your body to form a “Y” shape.
  • I Raise: Raise your arms straight overhead, close together, forming an “I” shape.

Maintain a neutral spine, avoid arching your lower back, and move slowly with control. Focus on squeezing your shoulder blades together and keeping your shoulders down away from your ears.

wger:1607.name: Typewriter Pull-ups
wger:1607.description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, slightly wider than shoulder-width. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar. At the top position, instead of going straight down, shift your body to one side by extending one arm while keeping the other arm bent. Move smoothly from one side to the other, like a typewriter motion, before lowering yourself back down. This exercise increases time under tension and strengthens the lats, biceps, and shoulders while building unilateral pulling strength.

wger:1608.name: Bodyweight Biceps Curl
wger:1608.description: Set up under a straight bar (around waist or chest height). Grip the bar with your palms facing you (supinated grip), hands about shoulder-width apart. Keeping your elbows high and close to the bar, pull your upper body toward the bar by flexing your elbows, similar to a biceps curl. Lower yourself back down in a controlled manner. Keep your core tight and movement slow to maximize tension on the biceps.

wger:1615.name: Treadmill Cardio
wger:1615.description:
It's a cardiovascular workout performed on a treadmill to improve endurance, burn calories, and promote heart health. It offers multiple benefits, such as the ability to easily adjust speed and incline, allowing for a variety of workouts, from hill walking to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) and tempo runs. To optimize results, it's important to vary your workouts. Benefits of Treadmill Cardio:

  • Improved Cardiovascular Health: Regular aerobic exercise on a treadmill strengthens the heart and lungs, which can help prevent heart disease.
  • Weight Loss: By burning calories, treadmill training can be an effective tool for weight loss and maintaining a healthy weight.
  • Muscle Strengthening: It strengthens the muscles in the legs and glutes, helping to prevent muscle loss, which is especially important with age.
  • Training Flexibility: Allows you to vary speed, incline, and intervals, making your workout more dynamic and adaptable to different fitness levels. Types of Treadmill Training:
  • Hill Walking: Increasing the incline of the treadmill and walking at a brisk pace can improve endurance and work your leg muscles.
  • Endurance Jog: A run at a comfortable, steady pace that keeps your heart rate in a target zone (such as Zone 2) to build endurance.
  • Interval Training: Alternating periods of high intensity (fast running) with periods of low intensity (easy walking or jogging) to maximize calorie burn and cardiovascular improvement.
  • Tempo Run: A run at a steady, sustained pace that is slightly faster than a normal jog, which challenges your ability to sustain a more intense effort for an extended period.

wger:1616.name: Dumbbell donkey kick
wger:1616.description: The dumbbell donkey kick is an effective exercise for working the glute and hamstring muscles. This exercise is usually performed on all fours, using a dumbbell to add resistance. The steps for performing it correctly are described below. Starting position: Get on all fours on a mat, with your hands aligned under your shoulders and your knees aligned under your hips. Placing the dumbbell: Take a dumbbell and place it behind the knee of the leg you are going to lift. Make sure it is held securely to prevent it from falling during the exercise. Exercise: Inhale and, as you exhale, lift the leg with the dumbbell upward, keeping the knee bent at a 90-degree angle. Raise the leg until it is parallel to the floor, feeling the contraction in the glutes. Hold the position for one second at the top and then slowly lower the leg back to the starting position. Repetitions: Perform 10 to 15 repetitions per leg, making sure to maintain good form throughout the exercise. Sets: Complete 2 to 3 sets, depending on your fitness level.

wger:1618.name: Stationary bike cardio
wger:1618.description: Benefits of Stationary Bike Cardio Stationary bike cardio is an excellent form of exercise that offers multiple benefits for health and well-being. Here are some of the most notable ones: Improved Cardiovascular Health Strengthens the heart: Regular exercise helps improve the heart's efficiency and reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. Increases circulation: It improves blood flow, which can help lower blood pressure. Calorie Burning and Weight Loss Efficient for burning calories: Depending on the intensity, you can burn between 400 and 600 calories per hour. Helps with weight loss: Combined with a balanced diet, stationary bike cardio can be effective for losing weight. Muscle Strengthening Tones the legs: It mainly works the leg muscles, including the quadriceps, hamstrings and calves. Improves muscular endurance: Over time, you can increase the endurance and strength in your legs. Mental Health Benefits Reduces stress: Exercise releases endorphins, which can improve your mood and reduce stress. Boosts energy: Regular physical activity can raise your energy levels and improve sleep quality.

wger:1648.name: Weighted Crunch
wger:1648.description:
The Weighted Crunch is a variation of the classic crunch exercise that involves adding resistance (a weight) to increase the intensity of the abdominal work.

  1. Lay down
  2. (Optional) Bend your knees to add difficulty
  3. (Optional) Bend your knees and let your feet rest on a bench or a box or something (90 degree angle on knees)
  4. Lift your head and torso while bending your back forward (if you don't it's a sit-up and also involves some back muscles). The higher you go, the more you should feel your abs contracting.
  5. Go back to starting position an repeat

wger:1672.name: Seated Hip Abduction
wger:1672.description:
Starting Position:

  • Adjust the seat height so that your knees are aligned with the pivot point of the machine.
  • Sit with your back flat against the backrest, maintaining good posture.
  • Place the outside of your thighs against the machine's padded levers.
  • Position your feet flat on the footrests or platform of the machine.
  • Grasp the handles or sides of the seat for stability.
  • Ensure your spine is neutral and your core is slightly engaged.

Movement:

  • Exhale as you slowly push your legs outward against the resistance pads.
  • Focus on initiating the movement from your hips, not your knees.
  • Continue opening your legs until you feel a strong contraction in your outer hips and thighs.
  • Hold the fully abducted position briefly (1-2 seconds) to maximize muscle engagement.
  • Inhale as you slowly control the return of your legs to the starting position, resisting the weight throughout the movement.
  • Avoid allowing the weight stack to touch down between repetitions to maintain constant tension on the muscles.
  • Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining control throughout the set.

wger:1689.name: Cable Fly Middle Chest
wger:1689.description:
Execution

  1. Start position: Arms extended out to your sides (a big “T” shape), feeling a stretch in your chest.

  2. Movement: Bring your hands together in front of your chest in a wide hugging motion.

    • Focus on squeezing your chest at the center.
    • Do not lock your elbows or turn it into a press.

  3. Return: Slowly open your arms back to the start, maintaining tension on the chest.

wger:1690.name: Cable Fly Upper Chest
wger:1690.description:
Execution

  1. Start position:

    • Arms down and slightly behind your body, elbows slightly bent.
    • Feel a light stretch across your chest.

  2. Movement:

    • Bring your hands upward and together in front of your upper chest — roughly at chin to collarbone level.
    • Use a smooth, controlled motion (avoid jerking).
    • Squeeze your chest at the top for 1–2 seconds.

  3. Return:

    • Slowly let your arms move back down and out to the sides, keeping control and tension.

wger:1691.name: Cable Fly Lower Chest
wger:1691.description:
Execution

  1. Start position:

    • Arms extended out to your sides in a “Y” shape.
    • Feel a stretch in your chest (slight bend in elbows — don’t lock them).

  2. Movement:

    • Bring your hands downward and together in front of your lower chest or upper abs, in a smooth arc motion.
    • Squeeze your chest hard at the bottom for 1–2 seconds.

  3. Return:

    • Slowly raise your arms back up along the same path until you feel a good stretch in your chest.
    • Maintain control — don’t let the weights pull you back too quickly.

wger:1693.name: Incline Static Hold
wger:1693.description:
Execution

  1. Hold Position:

    • Lower the dumbbells a few inches above your chest — about the midpoint of a normal incline press.
    • This is where your upper chest is under maximum tension.

  2. Static Hold:

    • Hold the position for 20–45 seconds while keeping the chest tight.
    • Breathe slowly but stay tense — do not relax your chest or shoulders.

  3. End the set:

    • After the hold, carefully bring the dumbbells down and rest.

wger:1694.name: Flat Machine Press
wger:1694.description:
Execution

  1. Start position:

    • Elbows bent at roughly 90°, hands just outside your chest.
    • Keep wrists straight and aligned with your forearms.

  2. Pressing phase (concentric):

    • Push the handles forward until your arms are almost fully extended — don’t lock out.
    • Focus on squeezing your chest at the end of the movement.

  3. Returning phase (eccentric):

    • Slowly bring the handles back toward your chest, feeling the stretch in your pecs.
    • Maintain tension — don’t let the weight stack touch down between reps.

wger:1695.name: Pull-Ups (Wide Grip)
wger:1695.description:

    • Focus on leading with your chest, not your chin.
    • Keep your shoulders depressed (avoid shrugging).

  2. Top position:

    • Chin should clear the bar (or at least reach bar level).
    • Pause for a brief squeeze in your lats.

    • Focus on squeezing your lats and upper back at the top.

    • Chin should clear or reach the level of your hands.
    • Pause briefly and contract your lats hard.

wger:1702.name: Jalón al pecho con agarre ancho
wger:1702.description: The lat pulldown is a pulling exercise that primarily targets the latissimus dorsi muscles (commonly known as “lats”) in your back. It involves pulling a cable bar or handle down towards your chest while seated on a machine specifically designed for this exercise. The lat pulldown is typically performed with a wide grip, but can also be done with a narrow grip or underhand grip to target different muscle groups in the back and arms. It is a popular exercise for building upper body strength and improving posture.

wger:1704.name: Tuck L-sit
wger:1704.description: The tuck L-sit is a bodyweight hold where you support yourself on parallel bars, parallettes, or the floor with straight arms while pulling your knees toward your chest. Your hips stay lifted, your spine stays tall, and your feet hover off the ground. The goal is to keep your core tight, shoulders depressed, and arms locked out while maintaining the tucked position. It’s a core-intensive, shoulder-stabilizing static hold often used as a progression toward the full L-sit.

wger:1734.name: Single-Leg Lunge with Kettlebell:
wger:1734.description:
How to do a single-leg kettlebell lunge

Preparation: Stand with your feet together. Hold the kettlebell with both hands by the handle, keeping it close to your chest, or hold it with one hand (on the same side as the working leg).

Step and Lower: Take a large step forward (or backward, which is safer for your knees) with one leg, lowering your hips until both knees form a 90-degree angle.

Focus: Shift your weight onto your front (or bent) leg, keeping your back straight and your torso upright.

Return: Push off with your front leg to return to the starting position.

wger:1735.name: Single-leg side glute press
wger:1735.description:
The Single-Leg Side Glute Press is a leg press machine variation where you angle your body sideways on the pad, placing one foot high and slightly angled to press the weight, powerfully targeting the outer glute (gluteus medius/minimus) and hamstrings for balanced leg development and stability, requiring focus on pushing through the heel and maintaining control without locking out.

How to Perform:

Setup: Sit in the leg press machine, rotate your body to one hip, placing one foot high on the platform at about a 45-degree angle with toes pointed slightly out/forward.

Positioning: Keep your hip, knee, and ankle aligned, and ensure your lower back stays on the pad.

Descent: Slowly lower the weight, allowing your knee to bend deeply (near 90 degrees), feeling a stretch in your glute and hamstring.

Press: Drive through your heel (not your toes) to press the weight back up, squeezing your glutes and hamstrings, stopping just before your leg fully extends.

Control: Avoid bouncing and don't let your lower back lift off the pad; maintain tension throughout the movement.

wger:1736.name: Single-Leg Deadlift with Dumbbell
wger:1736.description:
Starting Position: Stand upright with a slight bend in your knees, holding a dumbbell in one or both hands. Shift your weight onto your supporting leg (e.g., your right leg) and lift your non-supporting foot slightly off the floor.

The Hinge: Keeping your back flat and core engaged, hinge at your hips, pushing your glutes backward. As your torso lowers, extend your non-supporting leg straight back behind you for balance, keeping your hips square to the floor. The dumbbell(s) should lower toward the ground along the line of your supporting leg.

Range of Motion: Continue lowering your torso until it is nearly parallel to the floor, or you feel an intense stretch in your supporting hamstring, ensuring your back remains neutral throughout the movement.

Return to Start: Pause at the bottom, then contract your glutes and hamstrings to slowly raise your torso back to the starting position. Your non-supporting leg should return in line with the supporting one.

Switch Sides: After completing your desired number of repetitions on one side, switch your weight and repeat the movement on the other leg.

wger:1744.name: Machine Side Lateral Raises
wger:1744.description:
Machine side lateral raises are an isolation exercise for the side (lateral) deltoids, performed on a machine for stability, targeting the outer shoulder by lifting pads or handles out to the sides to shoulder height, then lowering slowly, keeping elbows slightly bent and traps down to focus on the delts. This exercise helps build shoulder width by preventing swinging and providing constant tension, making it great for beginners or as a finisher.

How to Perform Machine Lateral Raises

Setup: Adjust the seat so your shoulders align with the machine's pivot point, your chest is against the pad (or back if facing out), and your arms are at a 90-degree angle with the pads/handles.

Starting Position: Grip the handles with a relaxed grip, elbows slightly bent, and shoulders down (depressed) away from your ears.

Lifting Phase: Exhale and lift your arms out to the sides, moving your upper arms laterally, until they are parallel to the floor.

Peak Contraction: Pause briefly at the top, squeezing the side delts, but don't shrug your shoulders up.

Lowering Phase: Inhale and slowly lower the weight back down with control, resisting the weight on the way down.

wger:1745.name: Cable Front Raise with a small bar
wger:1745.description:
The Cable Front Raise with a small bar isolates your anterior deltoids (front shoulders) by providing constant tension, requiring you to stand facing away from a low pulley, grab the bar with an overhand grip, and lift it in front of you to shoulder height with slightly bent arms, avoiding swinging and keeping your core tight for controlled movement up and down. Use a light-to-moderate weight, focusing on slow, controlled reps to feel the muscle work, not momentum.

How to Perform the Cable Front Raise (Bar)

Setup: Attach a small straight bar to a low cable pulley. Set the weight to a light or moderate setting.

Starting Position: Stand with your back to the machine, holding the bar with an overhand grip (palms facing down) at hip level, arms extended but not locked. Feet shoulder-width apart, core braced, shoulders back and down.

The Lift: Exhale and slowly raise the bar straight up in front of you, keeping a slight bend in your elbows, until your hands reach shoulder height (or slightly below).

The Hold: Pause briefly at the top, squeezing your front delts.

The Lower: Inhale as you slowly and controllably lower the bar back to the starting position, maintaining tension.

wger:1748.name: Machine Hip Abduction
wger:1748.description:
Technique and Execution

Starting Position

Seated Positioning: Sit in the machine with back against the pad

Leg Placement: Inner thighs against the machine's padded resistance points

Adjust Machine: Set seat position to align your hip joint with the machine's pivot point

Movement Technique

Start with legs together or slightly pressed against the inner pads

Slowly push legs outward, spreading them apart

Move until maximum comfortable lateral range is reached

Pause briefly at the outer point of the movement

Slowly return to the starting position with controlled movement

Biomechanical Breakdown

Muscle Engagement

Primary Activation: Gluteus Medius (side hip muscle)

Stabilization: Engages core and lower back muscles

Functional Movement: Mimics lateral leg movement used in walking, sports, and daily activities

Benefits

Strength and Stability

Improves Hip Stability

Reduces Risk of Knee Injuries

Enhances Lateral Movement Capabilities

Targets Often-Neglected Muscle Groups

wger:1751.name: Cable pull through
wger:1751.description:
The Cable Pull Through is a lower-body exercise that targets the glutes and hamstrings using a "hip hinge" motion. To perform it, attach a rope to the lowest pulley setting, face away from the machine with the rope between your legs, and step forward to create tension. Keeping your back flat and knees slightly soft, push your hips backward as if trying to close a door behind you until you feel a deep stretch in your hamstrings.

To finish the rep, explosively drive your hips forward to return to a standing position, squeezing your glutes hard at the top. It is vital to remember that this is not a squat; your knees should not bend deeply, and your arms should remain straight and relaxed, acting only as hooks for the rope. This movement provides constant tension on the glutes while placing less stress on the lower back than a traditional deadlift.

wger:1822.name: Open Book
wger:1822.description:
Basic exercise

  • Focus: enhances thoracic mobility and spinal segmentation while opening the shoulders and chest.
  • **Position:**kneeling on the floor with your right side facing a wall. Hips are square and stable, with the right knee down and the left foot forward. Lengthen your spine and align your head comfortably. Begin with your arms relaxed and open in front of your chest, palms facing each other and hands apart.
  • Inhale to initiate the movement, allowing your left arm —the one farther from the wall— to open outward and backward. Lead the twist from your thoracic spine, rotating your upper back progressively while keeping your pelvis still.
  • Exhale as you complete the rotation, guiding your left hand toward the wall as your gaze follows your hand.
  • Return by inhaling and slowly bringing your arm forward, reversing the spinal rotation segment by segment.
  • Repeat on the opposite side.

Progression

  • **Position:**kneeling on the floor with your right side facing a wall. Left knee down and right foot forward.
  • Before the basic exercise: inhale, exhalewhile moving the right arm along the wall with a circle upwards and backwards, inhalewhile bringing back the arm.
  • Basic exercise.
  • Repeat on the opposite side.

wger:1824.name: Dumbell Tate Press
wger:1824.description:
1. Set Up: Lie flat with a dumbbell in each hand. Extend your arms straight up over your chest as if you were at the top of a dumbbell bench press
  2. Starting Position: Position the dumbbells so they are touching or very close together with a pronated grip (palms facing your feet and thumbs facing each other)
  3. Lowering: Without moving your upper arms or shoulders, bend your elbows and flare them outward to the sides. Lower the inner ends of the dumbbells toward the center of your chest
  4. Touch and Pause: Gently touch the dumbbells to your chest. Do not rest the weight on your body; maintain constant tension in your triceps
  5. Press: Forcefully extend your elbows to return the dumbbells to the starting position. Focus on "pushing your pinkies toward the sky" to maximize triceps engagement

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IgSjoXbpy1M&t=2

wger:1826.name: Band pull-apart with external rotation
wger:1826.description:
Stand tall with your feet shoulder-width apart, chest out, and shoulders back.

Hold the resistance band with both hands, palms facing up or facing each other, depending on the band type.

Bend your elbows at a 90-degree angle and glue your upper arms to your sides.

The band should have some tension in the starting position, with your hands closer together in front of your stomach.

Rotate Outward: While keeping your elbows tucked into your sides, slowly move your hands away from each other, stretching the band.

Squeeze: Squeeze your shoulder blades together and down as you rotate your hands outward.

Range of Motion: Rotate your hands as far outward as you comfortably can without allowing your elbows to leave your sides.

Hold: Hold the end position for 1–2 seconds to maximize muscle engagement.

Return: Slowly and with control, bring your hands back to the starting position.

wger:1829.name: Landmine Squat to Press
wger:1829.description:
Bar Position: Anchor one end of a barbell in a landmine attachment or a secure corner. Stance: Stand facing the barbell with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Turn your toes out 10–35 degrees to allow for better pelvic movement and depth. Grip: Cup the free end of the barbell with both hands (fingers interlaced or overlapping) and hold it at mid-chest level, just below the collarbone.

Descent: Brace your core and sit back into a squat, keeping your chest up and weight on your heels. Depth: Lower until your thighs are at least parallel to the floor. A good reference is when your elbows touch the tops of your thighs or just inside your knees. Posture: Ensure your back remains flat and your spine neutral throughout the movement.

Drive: Powerfully drive through your heels to stand up. Use the momentum from your legs to "thrust" the weight upward. Extension: In one fluid motion, press the bar overhead until your arms are fully extended. At the top, your biceps should be near your ears. The "Lean": As you reach the top of the press, lean slightly forward into the bar to encourage proper upward rotation of the shoulder blades and avoid lower back arching.

Slowly lower the barbell back to chest height in a controlled manner before immediately beginning the next repetition.

wger:1879.name: Incline DB Y-Raise
wger:1879.description:
1. Set an incline bench to a 45-degree angle and sit facing the bench, chest against the pad, with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing each other.
  2. Position your feet firmly on the ground for stability and let your arms hang down naturally with a slight bend in your elbows.
  3. Engage your core and keep your back straight throughout the movement.
  4. Raise your arms forward and out to form a Y shape, keeping the movement controlled and your elbows slightly bent.
  5. Lift until your arms are roughly parallel to the floor and in line with your ears.
  6. Pause briefly at the top of the movement to engage your shoulder muscles fully, then slowly lower your arms back down to the starting position.
  7. Ensure the movement is slow and controlled during both the ascent and descent to maximize engagement of the deltoids and supporting muscles.
  8. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions, maintaining proper form throughout.

wger:1882.name: High-Cable Lateral Raise
wger:1882.description:
Stand next to a cable machine with the pulley set to waist height.

Grab the opposite-side handle with the hand farthest from the pulley, keeping your palm facing in.

Keep your core engaged, chest lifted, and shoulders relaxed. Maintain a slight bend in the elbow throughout the lift.

Lift your arm out to the side until your elbow reaches shoulder height, keeping your wrist aligned with your elbow.

Briefly pause at the top, then slowly lower the handle back to your side with control. Repeat for the desired reps.

wger:1884.name: Shinbox IR Stretch
wger:1884.description:
• Starting Position: Sit on the floor with both hips and knees bent at 90-degree angles.
  • Leg Placement: Place one leg in front of you (external rotation) and the other leg out to the side/behind you (internal rotation). The shins and knees should remain flat on the ground.
  • The Movement: Keeping your hips square, hinge your torso forward or tilt it laterally (side-to-side) toward the front leg to deepen the stretch.
  • Target Areas: Stretches the glutes and piriformis (front leg) and the hip flexors and quads (back leg). Engages the core and obliques during lateral flexion.
  • Goal: Improves hip mobility, specifically internal and external rotation, and relieves lower back tension.

* **The Movement:**

wger:1885.name: YTWL Exercise
wger:1885.description:
• Purpose: Improves shoulder stability, posture, and scapular (shoulder blade) control. Often used in physical therapy and warm-ups.
  • Starting Position: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips (like a deadlift) keeping your back flat, or lie face down on an incline bench. Keep your thumbs pointing up throughout.
  • Y (Arms up): Extend both arms straight forward and upward at a 135-degree angle from your body, forming a "Y". Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
  • T (Arms out): Open your arms straight out to the sides, perpendicular to your body, forming a "T". Focus on pinching your shoulder blades.
  • W (Arms bent): Pull your elbows back, bending them to 90 degrees, and squeeze your shoulder blades to form a "W". Keep your wrists firm.
  • L (Arms rotated): Start with elbows bent at 90 degrees and close to your body. Rotate your forearms outward (external rotation) like a goalpost, forming an "L" or a gate.
  • Key Focus: Movements should be slow and controlled. Always lead with the thumbs and think about moving the shoulder blades, not just the arms.

wger:1886.name: Supine Hip Abduction
wger:1886.description:
• Starting Position: Lie on your back (supine) on a mat, with your legs extended and relaxed. Arms can be placed alongside your body or out to the sides for stability.
  • The Movement: Slightly lift one leg off the floor (keeping it straight or with a slight bend). Move it laterally outward, away from the other leg, as if stepping over a small obstacle.
  • Range of Motion: Move the leg as far as comfortable without lifting your pelvis or rotating your torso, feeling a stretch in the inner thigh and hip.
  • Return: Slowly bring the leg back to the starting position with controlled movement.
  • Goal: Improves lateral hip mobility (abduction) and strengthens the pelvic stabilizer muscles.

  • The Lift: Raise your legs toward the ceiling using your abs, not momentum.
  • The Squeeze: Pause and contract your lower abdominals at the top.
  • The Return: Lower your legs slowly to the starting position with control.

  • Ascent: Press through your palms to return to the starting position, fully extending your arms.

wger:1928.description: The Seated V-Grip Row is a compound pulling exercise performed on a cable machine using a close-grip "V" handle. While seated with your feet braced, you pull the handle toward your midsection, focusing on back thickness and mid-back development.

wger:1929.name: Assisted Pull-Up
wger:1929.description: The Assisted Pull-Up is a compound vertical pulling exercise performed on a machine with a counterweight platform or by using resistance bands. It mimics the mechanics of a standard pull-up but reduces the total weight you have to lift, making it an excellent tool for building functional strength and perfecting your technique.

wger:1931.name: Dumbbell Curl
wger:1931.description: The Dumbbell Curl is a classic isolation exercise for the arms. Unlike the Hammer Curl, it involves rotating your wrists (supination) as you lift the weights, which allows for a full contraction of the biceps.

wger:1933.name: Abdominal Crunch
wger:1933.description: The Abdominal Crunch is a classic core isolation exercise performed on the floor or a mat. Unlike a full sit-up, it involves a smaller range of motion where you only lift your shoulders and upper back off the ground, keeping your lower back pressed firmly against the floor.

wger:1936.name: Cable Rear-Delt Fly (single arm)
wger:1936.description: Cable rear delt fly (single arm): Stand sideways to a cable machine with the handle set around shoulder height. With a slight bend in the elbow, pull the handle out and back in a wide arc so the upper arm moves away from the body. Keep your torso still and focus on the rear delt doing the work. Use light to moderate weight and controlled reps.

wger:1947.name: dumbbell snatch
wger:1947.description:
Key Steps to Execute Correctly:

Setup: Place the dumbbell between your feet, with your shoulders above your hips, chest up, and back flat.

The Pull: Explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles (triple extension) to drive the dumbbell upward, keeping your elbow high and the dumbbell close to your body.

The Catch: Quickly flex your hips and knees to drop under the dumbbell and receive it overhead with your arm locked in position, landing in a half-squat stance.

Common Mistakes: Using your arms too much to lift the weight instead of your legs, having a low elbow during the pull phase, and misaligning your shoulder, elbow, and wrist in the final position. For beginners, it’s recommended to start with light loads, focus on technique, and perform 3 to 5 sets of 3 to 5 reps per arm.

wger:1948.name: 1 Leg Box Squat
wger:1948.description: This exercise requires a sturdy box or a chair. Simple stand ~6 inches in front of it and balance yourself on one leg. From here, begin squatting down in a smooth controlled motion while keeping your other leg straight out in front of you for balance. Slowly sit down on the box, pause for a 1 count and push back up with the working leg, while never letting your other leg touch the ground.

wger:1962.name: Step Jack
wger:1962.description:
The Step Jack is a low-impact plyometric-style move that provides cardiovascular benefits without the joint stress of jumping. It works the entire body, specifically targeting the legs, core, and shoulders. This move is ideal for beginners, individuals with joint sensitivities, or as a dynamic warm-up to gradually elevate the heart rate. Notes (Instructions):

  1. ​Stand upright with your feet together and arms at your sides.
  2. ​Step your right foot out to the side while simultaneously swinging both arms up above your head.
  3. Bring your right foot back to the center and lower your arms.
  4. ​Immediately repeat the movement, stepping out with your left foot.
  5. ​Continue alternating sides at a steady, rhythmic pace.

wger:1963.name: Slow Squat
wger:1963.description:
​A tempo-based squat that uses controlled movement to increase muscle tension and improve lower-body stability.

  1. ​Lower: Descend slowly for 3 seconds.
  2. ​Pause: Hold at the bottom for 1 second.
  3. ​Stand: Return to the starting position at a normal pace.
  4. Form: Keep your chest up and weight in your heels.

wger:1964.name: Wide Push-Up
wger:1964.description:
​A push-up variation with a wider hand placement to increase the emphasis on the outer chest muscles and shoulders.

  1. ​Setup: Place hands wider than shoulder-width apart on the floor.
  2. Lower: Descend until your chest nearly touches the floor, keeping your core tight.
  3. ​Push: Drive through your palms to return to the start position.
  4. ​Form: Don't let your lower back sag; keep a straight line from head to heels.

wger:1965.name: Marching High Knees
wger:1965.description:
A low-impact cardio and mobility exercise that strengthens the hip flexors and improves balance.

  1. ​Movement: Stand tall and lift one knee toward your chest as high as comfortable.
  2. ​Arms: Swing the opposite arm forward as you lift your knee, similar to a walking motion.
  3. ​Core: Keep your abs engaged to maintain an upright posture.
  4. ​Pace: Perform the movement with control, alternating legs rhythmically.

wger:1966.description:

  • With both hands directly in front of you, rotate one arm open attempting to reach the wall behind you.
  • Exhale as you rotate, inhale as you return to neutral and repeat.

wger:1968.description: Press the dumbbell vertically overhead in a controlled motion until your arm is fully extended, without locking the elbow. Slowly lower the dumbbell back to the starting position at shoulder height.

wger:1969.name: Single-arm cable pushdown
wger:1969.description: Single-arm cable pushdown is a unilateral isolation exercise that targets the triceps brachii. By working one arm at a time, it helps correct strength imbalances between sides while also engaging the core for stability. Starting position: Stand facing the cable machine with your feet shoulder-width apart. Attach a single handle to the high pulley. Grab the handle with one hand using an overhand grip (pronated), with your elbow bent at approximately 90° and tucked close to your body. Keep your core braced and your back straight. Execution: Push the handle downward in a controlled motion by extending your elbow until your arm is fully extended. Hold the contraction for 1 second at the bottom, then slowly return to the starting position.

wger:1971.description: Close grip front facing Pull down, while focusing on Biceps, Increases activation of biceps over the whole range, Avoid activating Lats.

wger:1972.description: Sit at the lat pulldown machine and grab the single handle with a neutral grip. Keep your torso stable, your chest lifted, and your shoulder blades slightly retracted. Start with your arm fully extended overhead, then pull the handle down toward your upper chest following a controlled, slightly diagonal path. Focus on engaging the latissimus dorsi while keeping the shoulder depressed and avoiding any torso rotation. Slowly return to the starting position, maintaining full control throughout the movement.

wger:2447.name: Hip Airplane
wger:2447.description:
Stand on one leg and lean your upper body slightly forward while keeping your back straight. Extend the free leg behind you so that your torso and leg form roughly one line. Slowly open your hip to the side by rotating your pelvis and upper body in a controlled way. Then close the hip again and return to the starting position.

The movement should mainly come from the hip. Keep your standing foot stable and avoid letting your knee collapse inward.

wger:2448.name: Reverse Clamshell
wger:2448.description:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your knees stacked on top of each other. Keep your feet together at first, then keep your knees touching while lifting your top foot upward. Slowly lower the foot back down with control.

Move only through the hip and avoid rolling your pelvis backward. The movement should be small, controlled, and focused on hip rotation.

wger:2449.name: Clamshell to Reverse Clamshell
wger:2449.description:
Lie on your side with your hips and knees bent, keeping your legs stacked. Lift your top knee into a clamshell position and keep the leg elevated throughout the movement. From there, alternate between opening the knee upward and lifting the foot upward, moving through hip external and internal rotation.

Keep the movement slow and controlled. Do not let the top leg rest on the bottom leg between repetitions.

wger:2452.name: Curl De Muñeca Con Barra
wger:2452.description:
This is a variation of the flat bench press designed to emphasize the clavicular head of the pectoralis major (the upper portion). By tilting the torso, the angle of the push changes, shifting more tension to the upper chest and shoulders, which helps achieve a more aesthetic, balanced, and three-dimensional development of the torso.

  1. Starting Position: Grip a bar with an overhand grip (palms facing up) at a width similar to your shoulders.

  2. Position on the Bench: Kneel in front of a flat bench and rest the backs of your forearms on it. Your wrists and hands should extend slightly beyond the edge of the bench to allow for a full range of motion.

  3. Eccentric Phase (Lowering): Lower the bar in a controlled manner by extending your wrists toward the floor. At the bottom of the movement, slightly spread your fingers to let the bar roll down a bit, maximizing the stretch.

  4. Concentric Phase (Lift): First, close your fingers to secure the bar, then flex your wrists upward explosively but in a controlled manner, bringing the bar as high as possible. Strongly contract your forearms at the top position for one second.

  5. Form: Keep your forearms firmly pressed against the bench throughout the exercise; only your wrists and fingers should move.

wger:2454.name: YTW Raises
wger:2454.description: The YTW exercise for scapular retraction is designed to strengthen the inter-scapular muscles between your shoulder blades, to help retract or pull your shoulders back, helping to maintain proper upright posture.
wger:2454.description_source: The YTW exercise for scapular retraction is designed to strengthen the inter-scapular muscles between your shoulder blades, to help retract or pull your shoulders back, helping to maintain proper upright posture.

notes.comment: Start in neutral standing posture.
Bring your arms up to roughly 135 degrees for the Y position, slightly in front of you, then bring your arms backwards by squeezing your shoulder blades together.
Concentrate on squeezing the shoulder blade or scapula contraction at the end range of motion, holding this position for 3-5 seconds. Then release.
Bring your arms down to roughly 90 degrees, rotate your thumbs outwards, and bring your arms backwards by squeezing your shoulder blades again with scapular retraction.
For the W component, keep your arms around 90 degrees, but bring them backwards in a slight W position
squeezing at the end range-focusing on the middle and lower inter-scapular fibers.

wger:2480.name: Easy Continuous Swim (Freestyle)
wger:2480.description: Swim freestyle at a relaxed, steady pace without stopping — think conversation pace, not racing. Focus on smooth, even strokes rather than speed or breathing technique; this is just to get your body moving and your heart rate up.
wger:2480.description_source: Swim freestyle at a relaxed, steady pace without stopping — think conversation pace, not racing. Focus on smooth, even strokes rather than speed or breathing technique; this is just to get your body moving and your heart rate up.

wger:2481.name: Kick with Board
wger:2481.description: Hold a kickboard with both hands, arms extended in front of you, face in the water (lift head forward to breathe when needed). Kick from your hips, not your knees, keeping your legs mostly straight with a slight bend and a steady, compact flutter kick. This builds leg endurance and keeps your body horizontal without needing to worry about your arms.

wger:2482.name: Bobbing Exhale Drill
wger:2482.description: Stand in chest-deep water. Take a breath, submerge your face fully, and exhale slowly and completely through your nose and/or mouth the whole time you're underwater — a gentle humming sound can help keep the exhale steady and controlled. Once you're empty of air, lift your head, take a fresh breath, and go back under. Repeat continuously. The goal is training your body that all your exhaling happens underwater, so all you need to do at the surface is inhale.

wger:2483.name: Wall-Hold Rotation
wger:2483.description: Hold the pool wall or edge with one hand, body horizontal at the surface, legs kicking gently behind you. Keep your face in the water, exhaling continuously, then rotate your head to the side — not lifting it up — so one goggle stays in the water while the other clears the surface. Take a quick breath, then rotate your face back down to neutral. This isolates the head-rotation motion without any arm strokes to think about.

wger:2484.name: Side-Kick Breathing (Kickboard)
wger:2484.description: Push off the wall on your side (not flat on your stomach), one arm extended forward holding the board or just extended, kicking continuously. Keep your head in a neutral position looking at the bottom of the pool, and when you need air, rotate your head sideways (one ear stays in the water, other faces up) to breathe, then rotate back to neutral. Swim a length like this, then repeat on the other side. This teaches the exact head position and rotation you'll use once full stroke breathing comes in.

wger:2485.name: Stroke-and-Roll Drill
wger:2485.description: Push off, swim a few strokes, and every breath roll fully onto your back for 2-3 breaths, then roll back into freestyle. This teaches you to rotate your body as a unit rather than just turning your head, and helps remove the fear of not having your face in the water.

wger:2486.name: Recovery Bobbing
wger:2486.description: Same motion as the Bobbing Exhale Drill, but done in slightly deeper water (so you're not touching the bottom) and at a slower, more relaxed pace — think of it as a recovery/reset exercise rather than a hard drill. Use it between harder drills to reset your breathing rhythm and calm down if you're feeling rushed or out of sync.

wger:2487.name: Cool-Down Swim
wger:2487.description: Swim at an easy, unhurried pace — freestyle, backstroke, or just floating/gliding — with zero focus on technique or drills. The only goal here is to let your heart rate come down gradually and your muscles relax before you get out of the pool.

wger:2488.name: Posterior Pelvic Tilt
wger:2488.description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor. Flatten your lower back against the floor by tilting your pelvis posteriorly, engaging your abs and glutes. Hold 5 seconds, release. This retrains pelvic positioning to counter anterior pelvic tilt.

wger:2494.name: Band Terminal Knee extension
wger:2494.description: This is an end range strengthening exercise for the knee extensors. Start by looping a band around the back of one knee and anchoring the other end to a stable surface in front of you. Stand in a split stance with the banded knee bent and placed as the front leg. Straighten the knee to pull against the bands resistance and maintain a contraction in your quadriceps for up to 5 seconds before releasing.

wger:2523.name: Serratus Wall Slide Stretch
wger:2523.description:
1. Stand facing a wall. Place your forearms vertically against the wall so your elbows and wrists are both touching it.
  2. Point your arms slightly outwards from "straight up".
  3. Protract your shoulders had, then slide your forearms up the wall until your elbows are about level with your chin.

wger:2525.name: Couch Stretch
wger:2525.description:

  2. Extend one leg backwards, resting your foot "laces-down" on the edge of the bench.
  3. Lower yourself until your rear knee is on the floor and you are in a lunge position, with your torso hanging forwards slightly.
  4. Brace your core, tense your rear glute, and straighten up your torso to vertical, under control. Relax and repeat.

Repeat for the other leg, too.

  3. Slowly and controlledly pulse your body up and down by about an inch. Repeat for required reps.
  4. Repeat for other leg.

wger:2528.name: Squat Sky Reach Stretch

wger:2616.name: Single-leg BOSU balance
wger:2616.description:
Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise

The exercise for balancing on a BOSU ball while standing on one leg is known as the single-leg BOSU balance exercise. This exercise is effective for enhancing balance, coordination, and core stability.

Benefits of the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
  • Improves Balance: Standing on one leg challenges your stability.
  • Enhances Coordination: Engaging different muscle groups helps improve overall coordination.
  • Strengthens Core: The exercise activates core muscles, promoting better posture and stability.
How to Perform the Single-Leg BOSU Balance Exercise
  1. Positioning: Stand on the dome side of the BOSU ball with one leg.
  2. Balance: Keep your opposite leg lifted and your core engaged.
  3. Duration: Aim to hold the position for 10-20 seconds, gradually increasing the time as you improve.
Progression Tips
  • Add Movement: Try reaching for objects around you while maintaining balance.
  • Close Your Eyes: This increases the challenge by removing visual stability cues.
  • Use a Ball: Catch or toss a ball while balancing to further engage your core and coordination.

This exercise is a great way to build foundational balance skills before progressing to more complex movements.

wger:2617.name: Quad Sets
wger:2617.description:
What Are Quad Sets?

Quad sets are a fundamental exercise used in knee rehabilitation. They focus on strengthening the quadriceps muscles located at the front of the thigh. This exercise is particularly beneficial for individuals recovering from knee injuries or surgeries.

How to Perform Quad Sets Steps to Execute Quad Sets
  1. Positioning: Sit or lie down with your legs straight.
  2. Tightening: Tighten the quadriceps muscles while keeping the leg straight. You should see the kneecap move upward.
  3. Holding: Maintain the contraction for about 5 seconds.
  4. Releasing: Relax the muscle after the hold.
  5. Repetitions: Aim for 10 to 15 repetitions, gradually increasing as strength improves.
Tips for Effective Quad Sets
  • Ensure no other muscles are contracting to assist the quadriceps.
  • Perform the exercise on a flat surface, like a bed or couch, with a towel or pillow under your heel for comfort.
  • It is recommended to do these exercises multiple times a day, especially during the early stages of recovery.
Benefits of Quad Sets
  • Restores Muscle Function: Helps rebuild strength in the quadriceps.
  • Improves Stability: Enhances stability in the knee joint.
  • Increases Range of Motion: Aids in regaining mobility after injury or surgery.

Incorporating quad sets into your rehabilitation routine can significantly aid in recovery and improve overall knee function.

wger:2618.name: Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps
wger:2618.description:
Overview of Hip-Out and Hip-In Lateral Steps

Hip-out and hip-in lateral steps are effective exercises designed to strengthen the hip abductors and enhance lateral stability. These movements are beneficial for improving coordination and overall hip function.

Exercise Descriptions Hip-Out Steps
  • Movement: Step out to the side with one leg, keeping the other leg stable.
  • Target Muscles: Primarily engages the hip abductors, including the gluteus medius and minimus.
  • Benefits: Increases lateral stability and strength in the hip area.
Hip-In Steps
  • Movement: Bring the leg back in toward the center after stepping out.
  • Target Muscles: Continues to engage the hip abductors while also activating the adductors.
  • Benefits: Enhances coordination and control of the hip joint.
Key Benefits of Lateral Steps

| Benefit | Description | |---|---| | Strengthening Hip Abductors | Improves muscle strength around the hip joint. | | Enhancing Stability | Increases lateral stability, reducing the risk of falls. | | Improving Coordination | Develops better control and movement patterns in the hips. |

Incorporating hip-out and hip-in lateral steps into a regular exercise routine can lead to improved hip strength and stability, which is essential for various physical activities and daily movements.

wger:2619.name: Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds
wger:2619.description:
Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises that focus on balance and stability by landing softly on one leg and holding the position. This exercise helps improve proprioception and can be beneficial for rehabilitation and athletic training.

Overview

Single-leg soft-landing holds are exercises designed to enhance balance, stability, and proprioception. They involve landing softly on one leg and maintaining that position for a brief period. This exercise is particularly useful in rehabilitation settings and for athletes looking to improve their performance.

Benefits
  • Improves balance: Enhances stability by training the body to control weight distribution on one leg.
  • Enhances proprioception: Increases awareness of body position, which is crucial for injury prevention.
  • Supports rehabilitation: Helps individuals recover from lower-limb injuries by strengthening muscles and improving joint stability.
How to Perform Single-Leg Soft-Landing Holds Steps
  1. Preparation: Stand on a stable surface or a box.
  2. Takeoff: Step off the box or surface with one leg, ensuring that you do not jump.
  3. Landing: Land softly on the target leg, allowing the knee and hip to bend slightly.
  4. Hold position: Maintain balance in the landed position for up to 2 seconds.
  5. Reset: Return to the starting position and repeat.
Key Points to Remember
  • Keep your chest up and engage your core for better stability.
  • Ensure your knee aligns with the midline of your foot during landing.
  • Focus on a controlled descent to minimize impact.
Conclusion

Incorporating single-leg soft-landing holds into your training routine can significantly enhance your balance and stability, making it a valuable exercise for both rehabilitation and athletic performance.

wger:2620.name: Reverse V-Squat
wger:2620.description:
Step into the V-squat machine facing the pad, the opposite way from the regular V-squat, so that your chest rests against the pad and your shoulders sit under the shoulder pads. Place your feet on the platform about shoulder width apart and release the safety.

Brace your core and lower yourself by bending your knees and pushing the hips back until your thighs are roughly parallel to the platform. Drive back up through the heels without locking out the knees.

Compared to the regular V-squat, the reversed position shifts the emphasis towards the glutes and hamstrings.

wger:2622.description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet about hip-width apart, holding one end in each hand in front of your thighs. Keeping your arms straight with a slight bend in the elbows, raise your hands forward to shoulder height, then lower slowly under control. Can be done with both arms together or alternating. Use a heavier band or shorten the band to increase resistance.

wger:2623.name: Plate-Loaded Lat Pulldown
wger:2623.description: Sit at a plate-loaded (lever) lat pulldown machine with your thighs secured under the pads. Grip the handles overhead with arms fully extended. Pull the handles down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back, squeezing your lats at the bottom. Return slowly to full extension. Resistance comes from weight plates loaded on the machine's lever arms rather than a cable stack.

Set the seat so the handles start above your head with arms fully extended.
Drive the elbows down and back rather than pulling with the hands.

wger:2624.name: Lean-Away Cable Lateral Raise
wger:2624.description: Set a cable pulley at the lowest position and attach a single handle. Stand side-on to the machine, hold the frame with your near hand and lean your body away so you hang at an angle. With the far hand, grasp the handle in front of your hips and raise your arm out to the side to shoulder height with a slight bend in the elbow. Lower slowly. The lean increases tension on the side delts at the bottom of the movement. Complete all reps, then switch sides.

wger:2635.name: Seated Band Row
wger:2635.description: Sit on the floor with your legs straight out in front of you and your back tall. Loop a resistance band around the soles of both feet and hold one end in each hand, arms extended and a slight bend in the knees. Pull the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows straight back and squeezing your shoulder blades together. Keep your chest up and your torso still rather than rocking backward to move the band. Extend the arms slowly to return. Because the torso stays upright and supported, this is a useful row when a bent-over position is uncomfortable, and it needs no anchor point.

wger:2636.name: FlexBar Wrist Extension
wger:2636.description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing down and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist drop, then extend the wrist to raise the bar, keeping the forearm still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. The resistance comes from twisting or bending the flexible bar, so a thicker or stiffer bar increases the load. Commonly used for wrist and forearm strengthening and for elbow tendon rehabilitation.

wger:2637.description: Performed with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar. Rest your forearm on your thigh or a table with the palm facing up and the wrist just past the edge. Hold the bar in that hand, let the wrist extend back, then curl the wrist up to raise the bar while the forearm stays still. Lower slowly, taking about three seconds. Works the wrist flexors, and is the companion movement to FlexBar wrist extension for balanced forearm strengthening.

wger:2638.name: FlexBar Tyler Twist
wger:2638.description: An eccentric exercise for the wrist extensors, done with a flexible resistance bar such as a Theraband FlexBar, and widely used in rehabilitation for lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow). Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.

Hold the bar vertically in the affected hand with the wrist extended. Grasp the top of the bar with the other hand, palm facing away, and twist the top hand to wind up the bar. Bring both arms out in front of you with the bar horizontal, then slowly let the affected wrist untwist the bar over about four seconds while the other hand holds steady. Reset and repeat. The reverse version, twisting in the opposite direction for the wrist flexors, is used for medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow). Move slowly and stop if the exercise causes sharp pain rather than the expected mild discomfort.

notes.comment: The working wrist does the slow unwinding; the other hand just holds position.
Take about four seconds to let the bar untwist.
Mild discomfort in the forearm is expected; sharp joint pain is not.
Reverse the twist direction to target the flexors for golfer's elbow.

wger:2664.name: Seated Knee Extension with Overpressure
wger:2664.description: A gentle stretch to restore full knee extension. Sit with one leg stretched out in front of you and the heel propped on the floor or a low surface, so the knee is unsupported. Place both hands on the thigh just above the kneecap. Keeping the leg relaxed, gently press down through the hands toward the floor until you feel a stretch behind the knee, and hold for about three seconds before releasing. The pressure should produce a stretch, never sharp pain. Repeat for the prescribed number of repetitions, then switch legs.

wger:2665.name: Banded Monster Walk
wger:2665.description: A banded walking drill for the glutes and hip stabilisers. Place a mini band around both thighs just above the knees, or around the ankles for a harder version. Stand with feet hip-width apart so the band is under tension, then sink into a quarter-squat with the chest up. Walk forward with small diagonal steps, pushing each leg out against the band and keeping the knees tracking over the toes rather than letting them fall inward. Walk forward for the prescribed number of steps, then walk backward to return, keeping the band under tension throughout.

wger:2666.name: Step Calf Stretch
wger:2666.description: Stand on a step or a sturdy raised surface with the balls of both feet on the edge and the heels hanging off, holding a rail or wall for balance. Keep the knee straight to stretch the gastrocnemius, or bend the knee slightly to bias the soleus lower down. Hold for the prescribed time, typically 30 seconds, without bouncing, then switch sides if stretching one leg at a time.

wger:2667.name: Single-Leg Balance with Eyes Closed
wger:2667.description: A balance and proprioception drill. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent and the other foot lifted clear of the floor, then close your eyes and hold the position. Without visual feedback the ankle and hip stabilisers have to do the work, so expect noticeable wobble. Stand within reach of a wall, counter or chair so you can steady yourself if needed. Hold for the prescribed time, then switch legs. Commonly prescribed in rehabilitation after ankle or knee injury.

wger:2668.name: Single-Leg Balance with Kettlebell Circles
wger:2668.description: A balance drill that adds a moving load. Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent, holding a kettlebell in one hand. Pass the kettlebell around your body in a circle, handing it from one hand to the other in front and behind you, while keeping your balance on the standing leg. Keep the hips level and the torso upright; the shifting weight of the bell constantly changes your centre of mass, which is what trains the hip and ankle stabilisers. Complete the prescribed number of circles, reverse direction, then switch legs. Use a light bell to start.

wger:2669.name: Bent Over Dumbbell Rows (Two Arms)
wger:2669.description:
How to Perform It

  • Hold a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral or overhand grip.
  • Hinge at the hips, pushing your glutes back, until your torso is roughly 45–75 degrees to the floor. Keep a slight bend in your knees.
  • Let the dumbbells hang directly below your shoulders with arms fully extended.
  • Keep your back flat, chest up, and core braced — avoid rounding your spine.
  • Pull the dumbbells up toward your ribcage/hips, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades together at the top.
  • Pause briefly at the top of the movement.
  • Lower the dumbbells back down under control to the starting position.
  • Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.

Key Coaching Cues

  • Hinge from the hips, not the lower back
  • Keep the spine neutral throughout — no rounding
  • Lead with the elbows, not the hands
  • Avoid using momentum or jerking the weight up
  • Control the eccentric (lowering) phase rather than letting the weights drop

wger:2671.name: Radio Taiso
wger:2671.description:
Video can be found here : https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SGPBSqxKGAc

Full-body mobility and dynamic warm-up routine (3–5 minutes) to prepare joints, muscles, and the cardiovascular system for workout.

Movement Flow:

Deep Breathing & Arm Raises: Inhale while raising arms laterally overhead, exhale as you lower them.

Knee Bends: Soft, rhythmic knee flexions synchronized with arm swings.

Arm Circles: Large full-range arm rotations forward, then backward to open up the chest and shoulder girdle.

Chest Expansion: Cross arms in front of the chest and open wide to the sides.

Side Bends: Reach overhead to stretch the lateral torso left and right with a smooth side flexion.

Forward & Back Bends: Gently hinge at the hips to reach forward, then return upright with a mild spinal extension.

Torso Twists: Swing arms side-to-side to rotate the spine and loosen the core.

Ankle Mobility / Light Bounces: Soft heel lifts or light bouncing on toes to warm up lower leg joints and tendons.

wger:2672.name: kelso shrugs
wger:2672.description:
Kelso shrugs are a variation of scapular shrugs designed primarily to train scapular retraction, with particular emphasis on the middle trapezius, rhomboids, and, secondarily, the lower trapezius. Unlike conventional shrugs, the goal is not to elevate the shoulders toward the ears, but rather to pull the shoulder blades backward.

They are typically performed with the chest supported on an incline bench, using either dumbbells or a barbell:

  1. Lie face down on an incline bench, with your arms extended toward the floor.
  2. Keep your elbows almost completely locked throughout the movement.
  3. Starting with the shoulder blades slightly protracted, retract them, trying to bring them closer together.
  4. Keep your chest firmly supported on the bench; avoid turning the movement into a row by extending your torso.
  5. Briefly hold the fully retracted position, then return in a controlled manner, allowing the shoulder blades to separate.

wger:2676.name: Weighted neck flexion
wger:2676.description: Weighted neck flexion is an isolation exercise designed to strengthen the anterior (front) neck flexor muscles by bringing your chin toward your chest against external resistance (most commonly a light weight plate, resistance band, or neck harness).
wger:2676.description_source: Weighted neck flexion is an *isolation exercise* designed to strengthen the *anterior (front) neck flexor muscles* by bringing your chin toward your chest against external resistance (most commonly a light weight plate, resistance band, or neck harness).

notes.comment: 1. Lie flat on your back on a weight bench with your neck and head hanging off the edge. Keep your shoulders firmly planted on the bench.
2. Hold a light weight plate (5–10 lbs to start) against your forehead using your hands solely to hold the plate in place, not to push or pull it.
3. Slowly lower your head back toward the floor in a controlled motion until you feel a mild stretch in the front of your neck. Avoid hyper-extending the spine.
4. Tuck your chin inward first, then curl your head upward until your chin approaches your chest. Pause for a second at top contraction before lowering under control.

wger:2679.name: Tyson push-ups
wger:2679.description:
Starting Position

• Feet: Place the soles of your feet flat against a vertical wall, with your toes or balls of your feet on the floor. • Hands: Position your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart, directly under your lower chest or solar plexus. • Body: Keep your core tight, glutes squeezed, and head in a neutral position. Your knees should hover a few inches above the floor without touching it.

Movement Pattern

  1. Lower Down: Flex your elbows (tucked around 45 degrees) to lower your chest toward the floor, stopping just a few centimeters short of touching the ground.
  2. Rock Back: As you press upward through your arms, push your hips backward and bend your knees, rocking your weight toward your heels while keeping your shins nearly parallel to the floor.
  3. Drive Forward: Explode forward from your lower-body/crouched position, shifting your weight back into the starting push-up plank stance to complete the repetition.

Key Tips for Proper Form

• Keep Knees Low: Do not let your knees or hips pike high up in the air; keep the motion low and horizontal. • Maintain Wall Contact: Keep the soles of your feet pressed against the wall so you don't lose your leverage. • Engage the Core: Avoid arching your lower back by tilting your pelvis backward and bracing your abs.

• Place a dumbbell next to a flat bench
  • Place your left knee on on the bench, and plant your left hand on the bench so it is under your shoulder.
  • Place your right foot on the floor in line with your left knee
  • Grab the dumbbell with your right hand, neutral grip.
  • Starting position, shoulders should be in line and back paraller to the floor
  • Slowly pull the dumbbell up, by pushing your elbow upwards, keeping it close to your body.
  • Do repeats on one side, then on the other.
